prs.title: Handle massive values in Retry-After when calculating time to sleep for
prs.body:
The method `Retry.parse_retry_after(...)` will accept any integer returned by the remote server in the `Retry-After` header when the server returns a number of seconds to delay for rather than an HTTP-date. This includes massive and invalid values, for example `Retry-After: 9999999999`. This value is passed back to `Retry.sleep_for_retry(...)` which then uses the value directly in `time.sleep(...)`. The type is checked but not the value.

Using values for `time.sleep(...)` that exceed `PyTime_MAX` results in an OverflowError being raised:

```python
>>> time.sleep(9999999999)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-3>", line 1, in <module>
    time.sleep(9999999999)
    ~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^
OverflowError: timestamp too large to convert to C PyTime_t
```

This minimal PR adds a sanity check to confirm that the value of the `Retry-After` header is < 2147483647 (2 ** 31 - 1) in value. While `PyTime_MAX` is a `INT64_MAX` this is still a relatively sane upper bound value. If the value exceeds 2147483647 a clearer and more descriptive exception is raised.

This issue was seen in the wild:

https://github.com/meeb/whoisit/issues/60

It's highly unlikely that actually sleeping for decades or centuries is desirable but that's a different issue. I don't believe there's a specified sensible maximum for `Retry-After` in the RFC, perhaps limiting this to `3600` or similar lower value would be sensible?

Currently, even with this PR, a semi-malicious server could add `if ($http_user_agent ~ urllib3) { add_header retry-after 5000000000; }` and lock up some clients that attempt to handle retries properly for over a century (or at least until the process gets killed).

prs.title: Switch deprecation warnings to `FutureWarning` and reschedule removals
prs.body:
The codebase contains a few deprecation warnings with unmet target versions.
We've recently discovered that warnings using `DeprecationWarning` were not seen by most users.

This PR proposes switching from `DeprecationWarning` to `FutureWarning`, the later should be visible by default. Python will print the first occurrence of matching warnings for each location.

Here's an example of a script using a deprecated function and its output:
```python
from urllib3.fields import format_header_param_rfc2231

def warn():
    print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.txt"))
    print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.pdf"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    warn()
    warn()
```

```
$ python format_header.py 
./format_header.py:4: FutureWarning: 'format_header_param_rfc2231' is insecure, deprecated and will be removed in urllib3 v3.0. This is not valid for multipart/form-data header parameters.
  print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.txt"))
filename="test.txt"
./format_header.py:5: FutureWarning: 'format_header_param_rfc2231' is insecure, deprecated and will be removed in urllib3 v3.0. This is not valid for multipart/form-data header parameters.
  print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.pdf"))
filename="test.pdf"
filename="test.txt"
filename="test.pdf"
```


Related references:
https://sethmlarson.dev/deprecations-via-warnings-dont-work-for-python-libraries
https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3744
https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3731

prs.title: Fix proxy_ssl_context ignored for HTTPS forwarding proxies (#2577)
prs.body:
Found this while debugging SSL issues behind a corporate proxy in #3782. In forwarding mode there's only one TLS handshake and it was always using the destination ssl_context instead of the proxy one. Tunneling already worked because it has a dedicated _connect_tls_proxy() call. 

Fix is a 4-line branch in connect() to pick the right context. Also added ValueError when ssl_context and use_forwarding_for_https=True are both set, per the issue spec.


Fixes #2577.



## Root cause

The tunneling path (`proxy_is_tunneling`) was already handled correctly by `_connect_tls_proxy()`, which explicitly uses `proxy_config.ssl_context`. The forwarding path, however, fell through to the shared `_ssl_wrap_socket_and_match_hostname` call that always passed `self.ssl_context`.

## History

The bug dates to 691679f7 (Sept 2020) when forwarding proxy support was first introduced — the forwarding path was added with `ssl_context=self.ssl_context` and never corrected.    

## Fix


```python
if self.proxy_is_forwarding and self.proxy_config is not None:
    tls_ssl_context = self.proxy_config.ssl_context
else:
    tls_ssl_context = self.ssl_context
```


## Tests

- Removed the `pytest.skip("Test is expected to fail due to urllib3/urllib3#2577")` guard in `test_proxy_https_target_tls_error` — that test now passes directly.
- Added `test_https_proxy_forwarding_uses_proxy_ssl_context` which verifies that an HTTPS forwarding proxy works correctly when only `proxy_ssl_context` is supplied (no `ca_certs` fallback).

prs.title: Fix parsing behavior for ambiguous paths
prs.body:
## Overview

This PR is an attempt to address #3352. When a URI contains a path resembling a schemeless URI, urllib3 raises a `LocationParseError` in the `HTTPConnectionPool`. The existing code already treats all `/` prefixed URIs as paths via `_encode_target`, discarding the parse_url result entirely for these cases. The `parse_url` call was never
needed here and only causes problems when paths like //v:h get misinterpreted as a schemeless authority.

Removing this will also resolve the broken URL handling (#6711) that was added to Requests to work around this case.

## Proposed Change

We can shift the call order at the beginning of `urlopen` to skip these URIs without changing the current semantics. Anything that starts with a slash is inherently schemeless, so we set destination_scheme = None and encode the path directly. This matches the existing behavior but avoids the crash.

In the context of `connectionpool.urlopen()`, a `/` prefixed URI is always a path because `PoolManager` has already extracted the host, port, and scheme. The `//` prefix only looks like a schemeless authority in isolation.

If these _were_ for some reason schemeless authority URIs (//host/path), they were already broken at this layer. The existing code runs them through `_encode_target` as paths regardless. Given schemeless URIs are marked for deprecation, it seems sensible to leave the current behavior as it is.

prs.title: Fix issue number for `FutureWarning` in the changelog
Extract test dependency group, deduplicate dev and mypy
prs.body:
Closes #3594.

## Summary

Introduces a dedicated `test` dependency group containing only what is needed to run the test suite — no profiling (`coverage`, `pytest-memray`) and no maintainer tooling (`build`, `towncrier`). Downstream packagers (e.g. Fedora, see linked PR in the issue) can install just this group to generate build-time test requirements without patching the contents of `dev`.

`dev-base` now layers on top of `test` and adds the maintainer/profiling tools, so `dev` and `dev-min-pyopenssl` retain the same final dependency closure as before. `mypy` also includes `test` instead of repeating its contents, eliminating the duplication called out in the issue.

This implements @pquentin's suggestion in https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3594#issuecomment-2997196389:

> Sure, that sounds good, we can add a new group called `test` and include it in `dev` and `mypy`.

## Equivalence

I verified via `uv export --frozen --only-group <name> --no-hashes` that the resolved package set is **byte-for-byte identical** for `dev`, `dev-base`, and `dev-min-pyopenssl` before vs. after.

The `mypy` group additionally pulls `pysocks`, `pytest-socket`, and `pytest-timeout` (because they now come in via the shared `test` group). `nox -s mypy` still passes with no changes — the existing `# type: ignore[import-untyped]` annotations on the SOCKS imports cover them. Happy to split `mypy` back out from `test` if you'd prefer to keep its environment leaner.

## On `idna`

@pquentin asked in the issue whether `idna` is still needed. I checked: it is.

- `src/urllib3/util/url.py:333` does a conditional `import idna` (try/except `ImportError`); without the package, `_idna_encode` raises `LocationParseError`.
- `test/test_util.py` exercises both paths: `test_create_connection_with_valid_idna_labels` requires the package to be present, and `class TestUtilWithoutIdna` (line 1093) uses an `ImportBlocker("idna")` to verify the fallback when it's missing.

The other places that mention `idna` in the source (`connection.py`, `util/connection.py`) use Python's stdlib `encodings.idna` codec via `host.encode("idna")` and don't need the package. So `idna` stays in `dev`/`mypy`.

## Test plan

- [x] `nox -s lint` — passes
- [x] `uv lock --check` — clean after the refactor
- [x] `uv export` diff for `dev`/`dev-base`/`dev-min-pyopenssl`: identical closures
- [x] `pre-commit run` on touched files — passes
- [x] `towncrier check` — fragment found and renders correctly

prs.title: Sync test/port_helpers.py with CPython 3.14 socket_helper.py
prs.body:
Closes #3719.

## Summary

`test/port_helpers.py` was last copied from CPython 3.9's `Lib/test/support/socket_helper.py`. Per @Calvin0125's investigation in the issue, the only change in the two functions urllib3 uses (`find_unused_port` and `bind_port`) between CPython 3.9 and 3.14 is the Microsoft documentation URL in the `find_unused_port` docstring — the old `http://msdn2.microsoft.com/...` redirects to `https://learn.microsoft.com/...`.

This PR:

- Updates the URL.
- Bumps the source-version comment from "Python 3.9" to "Python 3.14".

## On Calvin's secondary question

> If the intention was to look through the urllib3 test suite and see if any of the new functions in `socket_helper.py` 3.14.0 would be useful…

I checked. The new additions in CPython 3.14 are `create_unix_domain_name()` (Unix-socket helper), `_get_sysctl()` and friends (read kernel sysctls on Linux/FreeBSD), and `has_gethostname` (a WASI capability flag). urllib3's test suite doesn't bind UNIX sockets, doesn't read sysctls, and targets Emscripten/Pyodide rather than WASI for its WebAssembly path — so nothing additional is worth importing today.

## Note on the dropped closing paren

CPython 3.14 also dropped the closing `)` from that same URL line, leaving the surrounding parenthetical block (started with `(This is easy to reproduce on Windows...`) unbalanced. I kept the `)` here to preserve a well-formed docstring. Happy to drop it if you'd prefer an exact byte-for-byte mirror of CPython 3.14.

## Test plan

- [x] `nox -s mypy` — passes (83 files, no issues)
- [x] `nox -s lint` — passes
- [x] `pre-commit run` on touched files — pyupgrade/black/isort/flake8 all pass
- [x] `towncrier check` — fragment found

prs.title: Unfold obsolete folded response header values
prs.body:
Addresses the original obs-fold response-header case discussed in #1362.

Python's `http.client` preserves obsolete folded response header lines in
`HTTPMessage` values. This change replaces each RFC 9112
`OWS CRLF RWS` sequence with a single space before urllib3 or downstream
consumers interpret the value.

The normalization:

- keeps urllib3's `HTTPHeaderDict` and the original `HTTPMessage` synchronized,
  preventing cookie consumers such as Requests from re-emitting raw CRLF;
- preserves header names, ordering, duplicate fields, and parser state;
- uses a common-case fast path and a linear-time pattern for long field values.

The socket regression covers the original folded `Set-Cookie`, duplicate
cookies, every SP/HTAB combination around CRLF, mixed and repeated whitespace,
multiple folds, and ordinary headers. Focused unit coverage also verifies
adjacent folds and preservation of the original message's order, duplicates,
payload, policy, and defects.

This intentionally does not address the separate whitespace-before-colon/header
name validation scope discussed on #1362.

Validation performed:

- full local suite: 2,279 passed, 333 skipped, 4 xfailed;
- focused strict nox sessions on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14;
- pyupgrade, Black, isort, and flake8;
- towncrier changelog validation;
- source distribution and wheel builds;
- end-to-end Requests cookie extraction and subsequent request serialization.

﻿## Summary

- decode SOCKS proxy credentials parsed from `proxy_url` before passing them to PySocks
- use `partition(:)` so URL credentials with an optional password are handled consistently
- add regression coverage for percent-encoded SOCKS5 credentials and SOCKS4 usernames, plus a changelog entry

`parse_url()` keeps RFC 3986 userinfo percent-encoded. `SOCKSProxyManager` currently forwards those encoded bytes directly to the proxy server, so credentials such as `user%3Aname` or `pa%40ss` fail authentication even though the URL itself is valid. Decoding after the username/password split preserves the separator semantics while giving the proxy the intended credentials.

Fixes #3785.

prs.title: Strip fragments from absolute request targets
prs.body:
urllib3 could send URL fragments in absolute-form request targets for HTTPConnectionPool absolute URLs/absolute redirects and proxied HTTP requests, potentially leaking client-side fragment data to origin servers or proxies.

Relevant excerpts from the RFCs
> [3.2.2. ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9112#section-3.2.2)[absolute-form](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9112#name-absolute-form)
When making a request to a proxy, other than a CONNECT or server-wide OPTIONS request (as detailed below), a client MUST send the target URI in "absolute-form" as the request-target.
>  absolute-form  = absolute-URI

> [4.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-4.3).  Absolute URI
>   Some protocol elements allow only the absolute form of a URI without
>   a fragment identifier.  For example, defining a base URI for later
>   use by relative references calls for an absolute-URI syntax rule that
>   does not allow a fragment.
>   absolute-URI  = scheme ":" hier-part [ "?" query ]

prs.title: Preserve explicit port 0 in connection_from_url and HTTP/2 authority
prs.body: connection_from_url() and the HTTP/2 request authority build the port with a truthiness check, so an explicit :0 in the URL gets dropped and replaced by the default 80 or 443. This is the same handling #5071 corrected for URL parsing, pool selection, and proxy configuration, but these two call sites were left using `port or <default>`. Switching them to an explicit None check keeps an explicit port 0.

prs.title: Add assert_hostname and assert_fingerprint to SSL_KEYWORDS
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds `assert_hostname` and `assert_fingerprint` to the `SSL_KEYWORDS` allowlist so they are properly stripped when constructing HTTP (non-HTTPS) connection pools.

Fixes #5077

## Problem

When a caller sets `assert_hostname` or `assert_fingerprint` on `PoolManager.connection_pool_kw` and then issues a plain-HTTP request, the kwarg leaks past the `SSL_KEYWORDS` filter into `HTTPConnection.__init__`, which raises a `TypeError`.

## Fix

Add both to `SSL_KEYWORDS`, matching the existing intent of the filter.

## Verification

- Reproduced the issue with the reproducer from the issue report.
- Verified the fix: with the change, both kwargs are correctly stripped before reaching `HTTPConnection.__init__`.

## Disclosure

Prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); I reviewed and verified the change and test results, and will respond to review feedback personally.

prs.title: Drop request body framing state on 303 redirects
prs.body:
Following a 303 redirect, urllib3 switches the method to `GET` and drops the request body per RFC 9110, Section 15.4.4 — but the state that *describes* that body survives the switch. Two things go wrong as a result.

### 1. The redirected GET announces a body it never sends

With `chunked=True` (or an explicit `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header), the follow-up request goes out as:

```
GET /done HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8080
Accept-Encoding: identity
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
User-Agent: python-urllib3/2.x

0
```

A bodyless `GET` framed with chunked transfer encoding. Harmless against tolerant servers, but it is invalid framing for a request with no content, and strict servers and intermediaries reject it.

### 2. A file-like body makes the redirect fail outright

`body_pos` also survives the body being set to `None`, so urllib3 then tries to rewind a body that no longer exists:

```python
import urllib3

pool = urllib3.HTTPConnectionPool(host, port)
pool.urlopen("POST", "/", body=open("payload.bin", "rb"), redirect=True)
```

against a server answering `303 See Other`:

```
  File "urllib3/connectionpool.py", line 768, in urlopen
    body_pos = set_file_position(body, body_pos)
  File "urllib3/util/request.py", line 184, in set_file_position
    rewind_body(body, pos)
  File "urllib3/util/request.py", line 221, in rewind_body
    raise ValueError(
ValueError: body_pos must be of type integer, instead it was <class 'int'>.
```

The message is self-contradictory because it reports the type of `body_pos` while the actual failure is that `body` is `None` and has no `seek()`.

Both problems affect `HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen()` and `PoolManager.urlopen()`, so the top-level `urllib3.request()` is affected too.

## The fix

When the body is dropped, the state describing it goes with it:

- `HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen()` and `PoolManager.urlopen()`: reset `chunked = False` and `body_pos = None` in the 303 branch, alongside the existing `body = None`.
- `HTTPHeaderDict._prepare_for_method_change()`: also discard `Transfer-Encoding`. This covers the case where the body was framed by an explicit header rather than by the `chunked=` keyword. The method already discards `Content-Length`, so dropping the sibling framing header is consistent with what it does today.

## Testing

Seven new tests, all of which fail before this change and pass after:

- `TestContentFraming::test_303_redirect_drops_chunked_framing` — socket-level, parametrized over `HTTPConnectionPool` × `PoolManager` and over `chunked=True` × explicit `Transfer-Encoding` header. Asserts the exact bytes on the wire: the original `POST` carries the chunked body, the redirected `GET` carries no framing headers and no body.
- `TestContentFraming::test_303_redirect_with_file_body` — socket-level, both pool types, covers the `ValueError`.
- `TestFileBodiesOnRetryOrRedirect::test_303_redirect_with_failed_tell` — pins the behaviour that a 303 never needs to rewind, so an unrewindable body is not an error.

### One existing test changed

`test_redirect_with_failed_tell` used `/redirect`, which defaults to `303 See Other`. That meant it was asserting the buggy behaviour: `UnrewindableBodyError` raised for a body that never needed rewinding, because the 303 had already discarded it.

I pointed it at `status=307`, which genuinely preserves the body and so genuinely requires a rewind. This keeps the test exercising the path its docstring describes, and matches how its sibling `test_redirect_put_file` in the same class already selects `status=307` for body-preserving redirect coverage. The 303 case it used to cover incidentally is now covered explicitly by the new `test_303_redirect_with_failed_tell`.

## Relationship to #3779 / #3780

Issue #3779 reports the same confusing `ValueError` message from a different trigger: a user-supplied body with `tell()` but no `seek()`. Open PR #3780 proposes changing `rewind_body()` to raise `UnrewindableBodyError` instead.

These are complementary, not overlapping — different functions, no conflicting lines. Worth noting that #3780 alone would not fix the case in this PR: it would only rename the exception, because here the real problem is that there is nothing left to rewind at all. Conversely this PR does not address #3779, which is about a body urllib3 still intends to send.

## Checks

- Full test suite run before and after; the only difference is the seven new tests flipping from fail to pass, no regressions.
- `black`, `isort`, `flake8`, `pyupgrade`, and `mypy` clean on all changed files.

prs.body:
Closes #3677

### Summary of Changes

As discussed in #3677, `Retry` defaults to `backoff_factor=0` (no delay between retries). For production services, immediate retries can easily lead to thundering herd problems or exhaust API rate limits.

This PR clarifies and documents recommended retry backoff practices:
1. **`docs/user-guide.rst`**: Added a new **"Configuring Exponential Backoff"** subsection under *Retrying Requests* that shows how to configure `Retry` with exponential backoff (`backoff_factor`) and randomized `backoff_jitter` alongside common status codes (`status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504]`).
2. **`src/urllib3/util/retry.py`**: Updated the docstring for `backoff_factor` to explicitly recommend configuring a non-zero backoff factor (e.g. 0.5 to 1.0) and jitter in production environments.

prs.title: Avoid repeated response decoder initialization
prs.body:
I discovered this low-hanging fruit during a short research effort into potential urllib3 optimizations.
It avoids repeated `Content-Encoding` lookups after decoder initialization.

I benchmarked the way Requests uses urllib3 by reading responses in 10 KiB chunks.
Median CPU times, excluding socket I/O:

| Decoded response | Encoding | Before | After | Saving |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 KiB | none | 0.0168 ms | 0.0166 ms | ~0 (noise) |
| 10 KiB | gzip | 0.0349 ms | 0.0350 ms | ~0 (noise) |
| 50 KiB | none | 0.0370 ms | 0.0349 ms | 0.0020 ms (5.5%) |
| 50 KiB | gzip | 0.1088 ms | 0.1078 ms | 0.0010 ms (0.9%) |
| 1 MiB | none | 0.433 ms | 0.379 ms | 0.055 ms (12.6%) |
| 1 MiB | gzip | 0.590 ms | 0.562 ms | 0.029 ms (4.8%) |
| 10 MiB | none | 4.499 ms | 3.969 ms | 0.530 ms (11.8%) |
| 10 MiB | gzip | 5.314 ms | 4.761 ms | 0.552 ms (10.4%) |
| 1 GiB | none | 1,050.1 ms | 979.4 ms | 70.7 ms (6.7%) |
| 1 GiB | gzip | 700.4 ms | 643.2 ms | 57.3 ms (8.2%) |

The 10 KiB case needs one read; every multi-read case improved.

prs.title: Raise SSLError for non-hex fingerprints in assert_fingerprint
prs.body:
## Summary

`assert_fingerprint()` already raises `SSLError` for unsupported fingerprint lengths and digest mismatches. When a fingerprint has a supported length (32/40/64) but contains a non-hexadecimal character, `unhexlify()` raised `binascii.Error` instead.

Wrap that failure as `SSLError` (same pattern as the existing `OSError` handling in this module) so callers that catch `SSLError` for verification failures see a consistent exception type.

## Test plan

- [x] Parametrized unit tests for non-hex fingerprints of lengths 32/40/64 (plain and colon-separated)
- [x] Existing `test_assert_fingerprint_*` cases still pass (`test/test_ssl.py`: 56 passed)

Fixes #5211

prs.title: Speed up URL percent encoding with an ASCII fast path
prs.body:
Already-valid ASCII URL components currently go through percent normalization and a byte-by-byte encoding loop. Return them directly when every character is allowed and the component contains no `%`.

Components containing `%` continue through the general path, preserving escape normalization and the handling of bare percent signs. The general loop iterates UTF-8 bytes as integers and formats each `%XX` escape only when needed. UTF-8 and `surrogatepass` handling are preserved.

Related to #3454. The changelog entry is omitted because the underlying changes have not been released.

Validation on the revised patch:

- URL utility, connection-pool, and pool-manager suites: **732 passed, 6 skipped**.
- Fresh differential runs against base `278d98d7bf6c`: **245,312** comparisons with seed `20260906` and **245,473** with seed `424242`, all identical.
- Black, isort, flake8, and scoped mypy (`--follow-imports=silent`) passed for both changed files.

The existing tests cover valid ASCII, bytes input, Unicode, lone surrogates, valid and bare percent signs, and allowed-character containers. For direct private-helper calls, the fast path preserves a `str` subclass instance and requires `allowed_chars.__contains__`; production URL paths supply plain strings and the module's sets.

Fresh measurements for `ff7b286f1eb8`, with the lookup table removed, versus base `278d98d7bf6c`: CPython 3.11.15, Windows, i5-12600KF. Both variants ran in alternating fresh processes pinned to logical CPU 0 (`0x1`). Five samples per variant, a discarded warmup pair, and the median of each process's best of three timings:

| Case | Baseline (µs/call) | Revised patch (µs/call) | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Already-valid short path helper | 3.416 | 0.462 | 7.40× |
| Already-percent-encoded path helper | 5.081 | 3.240 | 1.57× |
| Unicode path helper | 4.892 | 3.073 | 1.59× |
| `parse_url`, API URL | 12.925 | 6.636 | 1.95× |
| `parse_url`, simple URL | 5.471 | 4.681 | 1.17× |
| `requests.PreparedRequest.prepare_url` | 40.416 | 25.659 | 1.58× |

All 14 measured workload medians improved. Background applications were active and some later samples varied substantially, especially request preparation; these are local URL-processing measurements, not network-latency or cross-platform guarantees.

<details>
<summary>Small standalone benchmark for checking the direction</summary>

Run this on the baseline and revised checkout in alternating fresh processes pinned to the same CPU. It reproduces three workloads; the table above uses the broader harness and timings will vary.

```python
import statistics
import timeit
import urllib3
from urllib3.util.url import _PATH_CHARS, _encode_invalid_chars, parse_url

print(urllib3.__file__)
cases = {
    "valid_path": lambda: _encode_invalid_chars("/path/to/resource123", _PATH_CHARS),
    "encoded_path": lambda: _encode_invalid_chars("/path/with%20space/and%2Fslash", _PATH_CHARS),
    "parse_api": lambda: parse_url("https://api.example.com/v1/users/12345/repos?page=2&per_page=100"),
}
for name, operation in cases.items():
    timer = timeit.Timer(operation)
    timer.timeit(10_000)
    samples = timer.repeat(repeat=5, number=100_000)
    print(name, statistics.median(samples) * 1e6 / 100_000, "us/call")
```

</details>

prs.title: Assert on the ALPN extension in test_tunnel_sets_http_11_alpn
prs.body:
`test_tunnel_sets_http_11_alpn` asserted against the whole ClientHello:

```python
assert b"http/1.1" in self.buf
assert b"h2" not in self.buf
```

`self.buf` is the entire record, most of which is random, so `b"h2"` turns
up in it by chance. Measuring 3000 handshakes locally (OpenSSL 3.0.13, a
517-byte ClientHello), 7 of them contained `b"h2"` somewhere, about one in
430. CI is worse: newer OpenSSL sends a post-quantum key share, so the
record is several times larger and the odds scale with it. I hit it twice
in 300 local runs of the test and once on Windows CI.

This parses the ALPN extension out of the ClientHello and compares the
protocol list:

```python
assert client_hello_alpn_protocols(self.buf) == [b"http/1.1"]
```

That is stricter than what it replaces, it checks `http/1.1` is the *only*
protocol offered, instead of checking its bytes appear somewhere in the
packet, and the failure message becomes readable:

```
AssertionError: assert [b'h2', b'http/1.1'] == [b'http/1.1']
```

rather than a hex dump of the ClientHello.

The socket handler now also reads until the record announced by its header
is complete, instead of assuming one packet. A post-quantum ClientHello is
big enough that this is worth not relying on, and an incomplete read would
otherwise just trade one flake for another.

### Verification

- 500 consecutive runs of the test, no failures.
- Reverting `ALPN_PROTOCOLS` to `["h2", "http/1.1"]` makes it fail, so the
  assertion still catches the regression it is there to catch.
- The parser returns the right protocol list for `["http/1.1"]`,
  `["h2", "http/1.1"]` and no ALPN at all, over 3000 handshakes.
- Full `test_socketlevel.py`: 122 passed, 8 skipped.

prs.title: Give the memory-limited response tests room for allocation noise
prs.body:
Several `limit_memory` marks in `test/test_response.py` sit within a rounding error of their measured peak, so ordinary allocation noise fails them. Two have failed on CI in the past day:

```
MEMORY PROBLEMS test/test_response.py::TestResponse::test_buffer_memory_usage_no_decoding[False-None-read1]
  - Test was limited to 10.5MiB but allocated 11.0MiB

MEMORY PROBLEMS test/test_response.py::TestBytesQueueBuffer::test_memory_usage_splitting_chunk[finish_with_get_all]
  - Test was limited to 11.0MiB but allocated 12.0MiB
```

Measured with `memray` on Python 3.13:

| test | peak | old limit | headroom | new limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `test_memory_usage` | 12.13 MiB | 12.5 MB | +0.37 MiB | 15 MB |
| `test_memory_usage_single_chunk` | 10.00 MiB | 10.01 MB | +0.01 MiB | 12 MB |
| `test_memory_usage_splitting_chunk` | 11.00 MiB | 11.01 MB | +0.01 MiB | 13 MB |
| `test_buffer_memory_usage_no_decoding` | 10.00 MiB | 10.5 MB | +0.50 MiB | 13 MB |

Three of them allow 10 KiB of slack on a 10 MiB allocation. That is not a memory bound, it is an assertion that the allocator behaves exactly as it did when the number was written.

Each of these tests guards against the body being retained a second time, which takes the peak to roughly 20 MiB, so there is a wide gap between the real peak and the regression being caught. The new limits keep at least a 5 MiB margin below a doubled body while giving noise 2-3 MiB instead of 0.01 MiB.

`test_memory_usage_decode_with_max_length` (10 MB) and `test_buffer_memory_usage_decode_one_chunk` (25 MB) are left alone: neither has failed, and I did not measure them.

### Verification

- `test/test_response.py` passes on 3.12 and 3.13: 169 passed, 45 skipped.
- 15 consecutive runs of the whole `memory_usage` family under
  `coverage run --parallel-mode`, as the CI session runs them: clean.
- Adding a genuine extra copy of the body to each test makes all six
  parametrizations fail at the new limits, so they still catch what they
  are for.

One caveat stated plainly: I could not reproduce the CI overshoot locally on either 3.12 or 3.13, with or without coverage. The case rests on the measured margins and the observed failures rather than on a local reproduction. If you would rather see the extra megabyte accounted for before widening anything, I am happy to dig into that instead.

prs.title: Read the request body in dummyserver handlers that ignore it
prs.body:
Follow-up to #5161, where @illia-v asked whether the body drain added to `/redirect` should go to the other dummyserver handlers as well.

## The problem

A handler that answers without reading the request body leaves it in the socket. Hypercorn then reads those leftover bytes as the start of the next request on that connection, and the next request never gets a response, a read timeout, or a hang for a client without one.

Six handlers left a body behind on at least one code path:

| Handler | Methods | Before |
|---|---|---|
| `/echo` | GET, POST, PUT | GET returns the query string without reading |
| `/headers` | GET, POST | never reads |
| `/multi_headers` | GET, POST | never reads |
| `/specific_method` | GET, POST, PUT | `request.values`, which parses a body only for form content types |
| `/successful_retry` | GET, PUT | never reads |
| `/upload` | POST | `request.form`, which reads nothing from a non-form body |

Each one now reads the body first, with `parse_form_data=True` where the handler goes on to use `request.form` or `request.values`, matching `/redirect` and the existing `pyodide_upload`.

## Why nothing noticed

A small body fits in the socket buffers and hypercorn discards it with the rest of the connection state. The desynchronization only shows up once the body is larger than those buffers, on this machine the threshold sits between 256 KiB and 512 KiB, which is well above anything the test suite sends.

## Verification

I checked each handler with a throwaway test that sent a 2 MiB body and then made a second request on the same connection, asserting the connection was reused. Six of its eight parametrizations failed on `main` and all eight passed with this change:

```
FAILED ...[GET-/echo]
FAILED ...[POST-/headers]
FAILED ...[POST-/multi_headers]
FAILED ...[POST-/specific_method?method=POST]
FAILED ...[PUT-/successful_retry]
FAILED ...[POST-/upload]
6 failed, 2 passed
```

The two that passed either way were `POST /echo`, which always read the body, and `POST /redirect`, which reads it since #5161.

That test is not part of this PR, per review, dummyserver is scaffolding rather than something to test in its own right.

`test/with_dummyserver/` is otherwise unchanged: same failure set and same pass count before and after.

## What I did not do

**A blanket `before_request` hook.** It is the obvious generalization, and I tried it first:

```python
@hypercorn_app.before_request
@pyodide_testing_app.before_request
async def read_request_body() -> None:
    await request.get_data(parse_form_data=True)
```

It breaks four tests. `parse_form_data=True` consumes a multipart body into `request.form`, so `/echo` then echoes back an empty body and `test_post_with_multipart` fails. Dropping `parse_form_data` instead breaks every handler that reads `request.form` or `request.values`, which is the original `/redirect` bug. The per-handler call lets each one ask for what it actually needs.

**`OPTIONS` paths.** `/echo_json` and `pyodide_upload` return early for `OPTIONS` without reading the body, but a CORS preflight does not carry one, and on the hypercorn app `/echo_json` is registered for `POST` only.

prs.title: Test pickling of `InvalidChunkLength`
prs.body:
`InvalidChunkLength` is not covered by the `TestPickle` matrix, and it is a natural candidate for it: the exception carries a whole `HTTPResponse` object in its `args`, which is exactly the kind of payload that can break pickling when an exception crosses a process boundary (e.g. multiprocessing or concurrent.futures workers).

The test builds a response that has been partially read, so that `partial`, `expected`, and `length` all hold non-default values, and asserts that each of them survives a pickle round trip.

prs.title: dummyserver leaks sockets when a port bind is retried
prs.body:
### What happened Some random tests on Ubuntu CI ERROR with: ```text ExceptionGroup: multiple unraisable exception warnings (2 sub-exceptions) ``` The two warnings are always: ```text ResourceWarning: unclosed ResourceWarning: unclosed ``` Both come from `dummyserver/hypercornserver.py`, in `_retry_create_urllib3_sockets`. Which test gets the ERROR is random. It happened in 12 different tests across 13 jobs. ### Why it happens `_retry_create_urllib3_sockets` retries up to 10 times when the bind fails with `EADDRINUSE`. Inside `_create_urllib3_sockets`, we go through the results of `getaddrinfo("localhost")` and create a socket for each one. We set the socket options, bind the first socket to port 0, and it gets a random port. Each later socket is then bound to that port. The problem is that if one of those binds fails, we don't close the sockets that were created during that attempt. In the CI Ubuntu runners, `localhost` resolves to `::1` first and then `127.0.0.1`. So in the failing case: 1. the `::1` socket gets port `P` from the kernel 2. we then try to bind `127.0.0.1:P` 3. the IPv4 bind gets `EADDRINUSE` 4. the retry starts 5. the socket list from the failed attempt is lost 6. the `::1` socket is never closed 7. the IPv4 socket whose bind failed is never closed either CPython later cleans up these sockets and raises the two `ResourceWarning`s. Since `pyproject.toml` has `filterwarnings = ["error"]`, pytest reports these warnings as an ERROR. ### How I reproduced it I first reproduced it with real sockets and a real kernel `EADDRINUSE`. I had a blocker listening on `127.0.0.1` at the port that `::1` had just received. Locally, `localhost` only resolves to `127.0.0.1`, so I only had to emulate the `::1`-then-`127.0.0.1` resolver order. That produced the same two unclosed sockets as CI. I then reproduced it end-to-end through a real pytest run in `test/with_dummyserver/test_connection.py`. The test injects one port collision during dummyserver startup, and a plugin records whether the collision actually happened. With main, each of 5 runs gave: ```text 29 passed, 1 error 2 unclosed sockets ``` The error was the same CI `ExceptionGroup`, with the same two sub-exceptions. With the fix, each of 5 runs gave: ```text 30 passed, 0 errors 0 unclosed sockets ``` Across all 10 runs, `collision_injected=True` every time. Each run had one failed bind with `EADDRINUSE`, followed by a successful retry. Separately, I checked the sockets returned after a successful retry. It still returns two open sockets, `::1` and `127.0.0.1`, and both use the same port. ### CI I searched the CI history from June 15 through September 16, 2026. The failures themselves happened in 13 Ubuntu jobs between July 1 and September 9. Five of those jobs are proven flaky because the same job also passed on the same commit. Two of the jobs were on main. The rate was about 1 in 393 Ubuntu CPython test jobs. There were no new occurrences from September 10 through September 16. CI example: - https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/31429999901/job/93590820201 Proven flaky jobs: - https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/30850679098/job/91809657780 - https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33895538431/job/101097170836 - https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33972110476/job/101322331392 - https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/34273101910/job/102219395742 As a separate check, exactly the same 13 jobs contain `Retrying binding to ...`. ### The fix The loop is wrapped in `try / except BaseException`. If anything goes wrong, all sockets created so far are closed and the exception is re-raised. Each socket is also added to the list immediately after `socket.socket(...)`. This means the socket whose `bind()` fails is also closed. The retry behaviour is unchanged. ### Checks The full test suite passes both before and after the change: `2396 passed, 309 skipped, 4 xfailed, 0 failures`. Black, isort, flake8 and pyupgrade are clean with the pinned pre-commit versions. Mypy is clean when targeting Python 3.13 and 3.14, which matches the latest Python used by the CI lint job. When targeting Python 3.12, mypy reports: ```text src/urllib3/connection.py:146: error: Final can be only used as an outermost qualifier in a variable annotation [valid-type] ``` The same error is present on unmodified upstream main, so it is unrelated to this change. ### Related PRs While looking into this, I found that the same change is already present in two open, unreviewed PRs: - #4999 - "Construct Authorization and Proxy-Authorization headers from URL credentials" - last updated May 20 - #5042 - "Update request header typing for bytes" - last updated May 23 In both PRs, this change is bundled with unrelated work. There are no reviews or comments about this change, and neither PR mentions the leak in its description. There is also no existing issue about this leak. This PR keeps the change focused and includes the CI evidence and the end-to-end reproduction. ### Why there is no test Illia said on #5239: > "I don't think we need dedicated tests for dummyserver itself" So I did not add a dedicated dummyserver test. ### A few things that may come up
Isn't this already in #4999/#5042? Yes. The same change is already included in both PRs, but it is bundled with unrelated work and neither PR has been reviewed. This PR is focused on this issue and includes the CI evidence and reproduction.
Why BaseException instead of OSError? It also cleans up on things such as `KeyboardInterrupt`. The exception is always re-raised. This is also the choice used in #4999/#5042.
Why only Ubuntu? I don't know. The retry message only appears in the Ubuntu logs. One caveat is that the message is only visible when a failing test prints its captured output.
How often does this happen? About 1 in 393 Ubuntu CPython jobs.
Does the fix change behaviour when there is no bind failure? The full test suite passes both before and after the change. The suite starts the dummyserver many times, including cases where there is no bind failure. The code on that path is also nearly the same. The change only adds the `try` wrapper and moves where the socket is appended to the list.
Why is there no test? This follows Illia's guidance on #5239.
The comment says IPv4 comes first. Is that still true? The comment at lines 39-41 is stale. The code follows the resolver order, and CI binds `::1` first. This PR does not change the comment.
### One unrelated observation The retry loop also silently retries on `OSError`s other than `EADDRINUSE`. It eventually raises `failed to bind socket` without the original error. This is not part of this PR.

prs.title: Fix flaky SSL socket termination test on Windows
prs.body:
## What happened

`test_ssl_custom_validation_failure_terminates` intermittently fails on Windows with:

```text
AssertionError: The socket was not terminated
assert False
where False = wait(0.5)
```

The same test is also run through the pyopenssl copy in `test/contrib/test_pyopenssl.py`.

There was no thread exception in any of the failures.

I checked CI from Jun 15 to Sep 17 2026. There were 15 failures, all on Windows, between Jun 24 and Sep 15. Eight are proven flaky because the same job passed on the same commit, and three happened on main.

The failure occurred on Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.14, 3.14t, and 3.15. There were no occurrences on 3.13. This is about 1 failure in 217 Windows test jobs.

The authors of #5249 and #5222 also hit the same failure on their PRs.

The eight proven flaky jobs are:

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/28471462074/job/84384922745

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/30303029543/job/90100365977

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/32984841906/job/98249021464

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33557044583/job/100020310500

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33895542413/job/101097183633

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/34835918191/job/103949597749

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/35006288030/job/104506744557

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33557044583/job/100020310404

## Why it happens

I found two ways to produce the exact CI failure by injecting the conditions into the real test on main.

First, the server can get `ConnectionResetError` during the TLS handshake instead of receiving the client's TLS alert. The handler catches the exception and returns without setting `server_closed`. The final `wait()` then fails regardless of how long it waits.

Second, the server can handle the TLS alert more than 0.5 seconds after the client has finished. `LONG_TIMEOUT` is 0.5 seconds on CI, so the wait times out.

I cannot tell from the CI logs which case Windows is hitting.

I couldn't reproduce the first case on Linux in 300 runs per test copy, even with a real TCP reset from the client. The alert that arrived before the reset was still delivered.

Since all observed CI failures are on Windows, the first case seems more likely, but that is only an inference.

There is also a report of Windows dropping received data when an RST arrives:

https://github.com/objeck/objeck-lang/issues/669

There is a separate report of Windows SSL tests intermittently getting `ConnectionResetError` because closing a socket with unread data can send a reset:

https://github.com/python-trio/trio/issues/1293

I have not independently verified either report.

## The change

The PR changes only the test in `test/with_dummyserver/test_socketlevel.py`, plus the changelog entry.

When the server gets `ConnectionResetError`, it now sets `server_closed` before returning. A reset from the client means the connection has been terminated.

The timeout is unchanged and remains `server_closed.wait(LONG_TIMEOUT)`.

Nothing else in the test changes. `is_closed_socket`, the `SSLError` branch, and the client side are untouched.

The pyopenssl copy gets the same fix because it imports `TestSSL` as `TestSocketSSL`.

The reset case is covered by setting the event before returning. The late alert case is not covered by this change. If the server handles the alert more than 0.5 seconds late, the test still fails as it does on main.

## Verification

I ran the two test copies on Python 3.12 five times and Python 3.14t twice for each case.

| Case                  | Main                     | With the fix             |
| --------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------ |
| Nothing injected      | pass                     | pass                     |
| Reset                 | FAIL with the CI message | pass                     |
| 0.6 second late alert | FAIL with the CI message | FAIL with the CI message |
| Real TCP RST          | pass                     | pass                     |

I also ran 300 runs per test copy with normal close and real TCP RST. All runs passed.

The full `test_socketlevel.py` and `test_pyopenssl.py` tests give:

```text
382 passed, 153 skipped, 2 xfailed
```

The same result as main.

Black, isort, flake8, and pyupgrade are clean. Mypy with Python 3.13 and 3.14 reports no issues.

## One separate issue

There is another problem with the termination check that I did not change here.

`is_closed_socket()` is always true because the TLS wrap detaches the original socket. This means the test passes even if the client never closes its socket.

I verified this by suppressing the client's `close()`. The test still passes on main and with this fix.

This is separate from the flaky failure, so I left it unchanged. I have a tested rewrite for this check and can open it as a follow up if the maintainers want it.

prs.title: Fix tautological assertion in test_default_pool_key_funcs_copy
prs.body:
`test_default_pool_key_funcs_copy` is documented as *"Assert each PoolManager gets a copy of `pool_keys_by_scheme`"*, but its equality check compares the instance attribute to itself:

```python
def test_default_pool_key_funcs_copy(self) -> None:
    """Assert each PoolManager gets a copy of ``pool_keys_by_scheme``."""
    p = PoolManager()
    assert p.key_fn_by_scheme == p.key_fn_by_scheme   # <-- always true
    assert p.key_fn_by_scheme is not key_fn_by_scheme
```

`x == x` holds for any object, so that line can never fail. The only thing the test actually verifies is the `is not` identity check on the following line — and identity alone doesn't establish that the copy carries the *same mappings*. A copy that silently dropped or rewrote entries would still be a distinct object, and would still pass.

`PoolManager.__init__` does:

```python
self.key_fn_by_scheme = key_fn_by_scheme.copy()
```

so the natural comparison is against the module-level `key_fn_by_scheme`, which is already imported in this test module.

## The change

```diff
-        assert p.key_fn_by_scheme == p.key_fn_by_scheme
+        assert p.key_fn_by_scheme == key_fn_by_scheme
         assert p.key_fn_by_scheme is not key_fn_by_scheme
```

One line. Together the two assertions now check the pair of properties the docstring actually promises: *equal in content, distinct in identity*.

## Verification

Mutating `PoolManager.__init__` so the copy loses entries:

```python
self.key_fn_by_scheme = {k: v for k, v in list(key_fn_by_scheme.items())[:1]}
```

| | original assertion | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| unmodified source | pass | pass |
| mutated source (copy drops entries) | **pass** :x: | **fail** :white_check_mark: |

Failure output with the fix applied:

```
E         Right contains 1 more item:
E         {'https': functools.partial(<function _default_key_normalizer ...>, <class 'urllib3.poolmanager.PoolKey'>)}
test/test_poolmanager.py:162: AssertionError
```

`test/test_poolmanager.py` passes in full (39 passed), and `black==26.5.1 --target-version py310 --check` reports the file unchanged.

Test-only change with no user-visible effect, so I believe this wants the `Skip Changelog` label — happy to add a `changelog/<pr>.misc.rst` entry instead if you'd prefer one.

prs.title: Avoid flushing swallowed gzip trailing garbage
prs.body:
Closes #5268.

When `GzipDecoder` encounters invalid data after at least one complete gzip member, it intentionally enters `SWALLOW_DATA` and ignores the trailing bytes. Python 3.14.8 now also raises `zlib.error` if that invalid stream is flushed, so the later decoder flush surfaced an error that urllib3 had already decided to swallow.

Return an empty result from `GzipDecoder.flush()` once the decoder is in `SWALLOW_DATA`. This preserves the existing trailing-garbage behavior without suppressing errors for the first gzip member.

A regression test replaces the underlying decompressor after reaching `SWALLOW_DATA` with one whose `flush()` raises, verifying that urllib3 does not call it.

Validation:

- Configured pre-commit formatting and lint hooks — passed
- Targeted type check of the changed files — no errors in either changed file (the repository-wide Windows run still reports existing platform-specific `select.poll` and `signal.SIGALRM` attribute errors)

prs.title: Handle ConnectionAbortedError in SSL socket test
prs.body:
## What happened

`test_ssl_failed_fingerprint_verification` intermittently errors on Windows because the server thread gets an unhandled `ConnectionAbortedError` while sending its response:

```text
pytest.PytestUnhandledThreadExceptionWarning: Exception in thread Thread-N

ConnectionAbortedError: [Errno 10053] An established connection was aborted by the software in your host machine
```

Some jobs print the same exception as `WinError 10053`.

The handler serves two connections, so the result depends on which `send()` fails. If the thread dies on the first connection, the second request cannot reach the server and the test fails as well as errors. If it dies on the second connection, the test itself passes but teardown still reports the thread error.

I checked CI from Jun 15 to Sep 22 2026. I found 5 jobs with this failure, all on Windows and all in `test_socketlevel.py`. Four are proven flaky because the same job passed on the same commit, and three happened on main.

The failures occurred on Python 3.13, 3.14, and 3.14t. This is about 1 failure in 750 completed Windows test jobs.

The most recent one happened on Sep 21 on main, in the run for #5266's merge commit. The rerun passed.

The five jobs are:

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/28947595607/job/85885406161

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/30495793430/job/90724163843

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/31377075102/job/93418641994

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33508700295/job/99858864660

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/35640521232/job/106468429516

## Why it happens

After the fingerprint mismatch, the client drops the connection and the server's `send()` fails.

On Linux I measured this without any injection. The `send()` failed in all 800 calls from 400 runs with two connections each. Every failure was `SSLEOFError`, which the handler already catches.

In the Windows CI failures, the same `send()` instead raised `ConnectionAbortedError` with error 10053. That exception is not currently caught, so it escapes from the handler and kills the server thread.

All 5 CI tracebacks end at this `send()` with `ConnectionAbortedError` 10053.

I don't know why Windows returns 10053 for this operation only sometimes.

The gap appears to come from #3240. That change added the `try` and `except` around this `send()`. The same PR added `ConnectionAbortedError` to the handshake exception handling a few lines above, but not to the new `send()` exception handling.

## The change

The PR adds `ConnectionAbortedError` to the existing exceptions handled around `ssl_sock.send()`.

The handler already catches `ssl.SSLEOFError`, `ConnectionResetError`, and `BrokenPipeError`. This adds only the exception seen in the Windows CI failures.

Nothing else changes.

The pyopenssl copy uses the same handler because `test/contrib/test_pyopenssl.py` imports `TestSSL` as `TestSocketSSL`.

## Verification

I injected `ConnectionAbortedError(10053)` into the server's `send()` on either connection and tested both copies.

I ran each case five times on Python 3.12 and twice on Python 3.14t.

| Case                       | Main           | With the fix |
| -------------------------- | -------------- | ------------ |
| Nothing injected           | pass           | pass         |
| Abort on first connection  | FAILED + ERROR | pass         |
| Abort on second connection | PASSED + ERROR | pass         |
| Abort on both connections  | FAILED + ERROR | pass         |
| Reset or broken pipe       | pass           | pass         |

When aborting both connections, the fixed handler survived both. All four injections across the two test copies were recorded in each run.

I also ran 300 stress runs per test copy with no injection and with aborts on both connections. All passed, including 1,200 injected aborts.

The full `test_socketlevel.py` and `test_pyopenssl.py` tests give:

```text
382 passed, 153 skipped, 2 xfailed
```

The same result as main.

Black, isort, flake8, and pyupgrade are clean. Mypy with Python 3.13 and 3.14 reports no issues.

With an abort on the first connection, the second request fails straight away locally, but with a different error than the Windows CI failure. The stdlib copy gets `NewConnectionError` or `ProtocolError`, while the pyopenssl copy gets an `SSLError` with a different message. On Windows CI, the second request instead reaches the 0.5 second connect timeout and gets `ConnectTimeoutError`. This difference does not affect the unhandled `ConnectionAbortedError` being fixed here.

prs.title: Skip TLS stream EOF test on PyPy 8.0.0
prs.body:
## Why this PR

The `pypy-3.11` CI job moved from PyPy 7.3.23 to PyPy 8.0.0 and started failing `test_tls_in_tls_makefile_rw_text` with:

```text
BufferError: Existing exports of data: object cannot be re-sized
```

The problem is in PyPy rather than urllib3. PyPy's SSL code kept a CFFI buffer export alive after `SSLObject.read()`. When a TLS stream is read to EOF, the bytearray is later resized and PyPy 8.0.0 raises `BufferError`.

The full investigation is in #5275 and pypy/pypy#5589.

PyPy has fixed the issue in commit `66c739f5370e` on its py3.11 branch, but there is no fixed PyPy release yet.

As discussed in #5275, this PR skips the affected test on PyPy 8.0.0 until a fixed release is available.

## The change

This adds a `skipif` to `test_tls_in_tls_makefile_rw_text` for PyPy 8.0.0:

```python
getattr(sys, "pypy_version_info", (0,))[:3] == (8, 0, 0)
```

The check matches 8.0.0 exactly. Once CI moves to a newer PyPy release containing the fix, the test will run normally again.

Using `getattr` also keeps the check working on non-PyPy runtimes without needing a type ignore.

The skip reason links to:

https://github.com/pypy/pypy/issues/5589

## Verification

With `CI=true` and the official PyPy builds from `downloads.python.org`, I tested the affected test on PyPy 8.0.0, PyPy 7.3.23, and CPython 3.12.

For the test alone:

| Runtime      | Main | This PR |
| ------------ | ---- | ------- |
| PyPy 8.0.0   | FAIL | SKIPPED |
| PyPy 7.3.23  | pass | pass    |
| CPython 3.12 | pass | pass    |

The PyPy 8.0.0 skip reports the expected reason.

For the full `test/test_ssltransport.py`:

| Runtime      | Main                | This PR              |
| ------------ | ------------------- | -------------------- |
| PyPy 8.0.0   | 1 failed, 16 passed | 16 passed, 1 skipped |
| PyPy 7.3.23  | 17 passed           | 17 passed            |
| CPython 3.12 | 17 passed           | 17 passed            |

Black, isort, flake8, and pyupgrade are clean. Mypy with Python 3.13 and 3.14 reports no issues.

There is no changelog entry in this PR, as requested in #5275. The changelog CI check may remain red until a maintainer applies the `Skip Changelog` label.

Closes #5275

prs.title: Prevent SIGALRM from terminating macOS test runs
prs.body:
## What happened

Some macOS CI jobs are being terminated by `SIGALRM` while running the EINTR tests in `test/test_wait.py`.

When this happens, pytest does not produce a summary. The last output is the name of the test that was running, followed by no result, and nox reports:

```text
Command ... failed with exit code -14
```

I checked every CI run and attempt from June 15 through September 23. I found 11 occurrences, all on macOS. Three are proven flaky because the same job passed on the same commit, and one happened on main.

That is about 1 failure in 345 completed macOS test jobs.

Ten happened while `test_eintr_zero_timeout` was running:

```text
6x [wait_for_socket]
4x [select_wait_for_socket]
```

The most recent occurrence was different. It happened in `test_eintr[wait_for_socket]` on macOS with Python 3.14t.

Examples:

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/28390038386/job/84114484104

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/33893024465/job/101089012051

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/34717305351/job/103616739159

Most recent occurrence:

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/actions/runs/35726770755/job/106742223892

## What I found

The three EINTR tests have the same general signal handling pattern.

They install their own `SIGALRM` handler, start an `ITIMER_REAL` timer, run the test, disarm the timer, and finally restore the previous signal handler.

The previous handler is `SIG_DFL`.

While the test's handler is installed, `SIGALRM` cannot terminate the process. For the process to die from signal 14, the signal has to be delivered while its action is `SIG_DFL`, after the previous handler has been restored or before another handler is installed.

I could reproduce the same exit behaviour with a small model that generates a `SIGALRM` while the test handler is active but delays its delivery until after `SIG_DFL` has been restored.

That exits with status 142, `128 + 14`, without a pytest summary, matching the CI failure.

This demonstrates the race that the change protects against, but I have not found why macOS CI sometimes delivers a `SIGALRM` at that point.

I could not reproduce the real failure on Linux. I ran `test_wait.py` 30 times under a load average of around 25 without a kill, in addition to 150 earlier runs with `--memray`.

The newest CI failure also happened in a free-threaded Python 3.14t job that does not run pytest with `--memray`, so memray is not required for the failure.

## macOS diagnostics

I ran two sets of diagnostics on macOS runners to try to reproduce the timing.

First I tested the timer cleanup sequence without pytest, coverage, or memray.

Across six macOS jobs there were about 5,300 cleanup cycles and around 157,000 signals delivered per job while the timer was active.

I saw no signal arrive after `setitimer(..., 0)` returned. There was also no `SIGALRM` pending at either the disarm or handler restore point.

A deliberately planted late signal was detected in every job, so the instrumentation itself was able to observe that case.

I then ran the real EINTR tests using the CI setup, including `uv`, coverage, and `--memray` on Python 3.12. This covered 12 macOS jobs and 720 pytest sessions.

The diagnostic self-test was detected in all 720 sessions, but there were no signals that would have killed the process and none of the repetitions exited non-zero.

At the observed CI rate of roughly 1 in 345 jobs, this is useful evidence but not enough to rule the problem out. It also suggests that running the EINTR tests by themselves is not sufficient to reproduce it.

`pytest-timeout` is another possible source of `SIGALRM` in the full test process because timeout-marked tests run earlier in the suite. I have not established whether it is involved.

## The change

This adds a module-scoped autouse fixture in `test/test_wait.py` that sets `SIGALRM` to `SIG_IGN`.

The EINTR tests still replace that with their own handler while they run. The difference is that when they restore the previous action afterward, they restore `SIG_IGN` instead of `SIG_DFL`.

This prevents a `SIGALRM` delivered outside the tests' own signal handling window from terminating the pytest process.

I chose this over only changing the timer cleanup ordering because the actual macOS timing is still unknown. Reordering the cleanup can handle a signal that is already pending when the timer is disarmed, but the process becomes vulnerable again once `SIG_DFL` is restored.

## Verification

I modelled late `SIGALRM` delivery by blocking the signal, generating one, and releasing it at the point where the OS would deliver it.

I ran each case three times on Python 3.12 and twice on Python 3.14t with `CI=true`.

| Case                                                                | Main      | This PR   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- |
| Nothing injected                                                    | 13 passed | 13 passed |
| Signal generated during cleanup and delivered after handler restore | KILLED    | survives  |
| Signal generated during the cleanup window                          | KILLED    | survives  |
| Signal generated after handler restore                              | KILLED    | survives  |

`KILLED` means exit status 142 with no pytest summary, the same process termination signature seen in CI.

The EINTR tests still verify that they were actually interrupted with `assert interrupt_count[0] > 0`.

I also checked that `pytest-timeout` continues to work. A timeout-marked test placed after `test_wait.py` still times out normally because pytest-timeout installs its own handler when the marked test runs.

The full test suite gives the same result as main:

```text
2396 passed, 310 skipped, 4 xfailed
```

Black, isort, flake8, and pyupgrade are clean. Mypy with Python 3.13 and 3.14 reports no issues.

Because the original failure occurs only around once per 345 macOS CI jobs, a green PR run cannot prove that the flake is gone. The change is verified against modelled late delivery, while the reason macOS CI occasionally delivers `SIGALRM` after the test's handler is gone remains unknown.

prs.title: Speed up single-value header handling in HTTPConnection.putheader
prs.body:
## TL;DR

- **Problem:** `HTTPConnection.putheader()` currently uses `any(...)` over a generator to detect `SKIP_HEADER` for every header, including the common case where only one value is supplied.
- **Change:** directly check the value when `len(values) == 1`, while retaining the existing generator-based path for multiple values.
- **Performance:** repeated local measurements showed about **9–13% lower Python-side request-construction time** for the tested 4–12 header workloads.

---

The sections below are intentionally more detailed and mainly document the reasoning, validation, and trade-offs behind the change. They are included for reviewers who are interested in the full investigation.

## What was happening

`HTTPConnection.putheader()` currently checks whether any supplied value is the `SKIP_HEADER` sentinel using:

```python
any(isinstance(v, str) and v == SKIP_HEADER for v in values)
```

This is necessary for the general multi-value case and preserves the bytes/str safety behavior introduced in #2141.

However, normal request construction overwhelmingly calls `putheader()` with a single value. In that case, the generator and `any()` machinery perform unnecessary Python-level work before the header is passed to `http.client.HTTPConnection.putheader()`.

The existing path is effectively:

```text
single header value
→ create generator
→ enter any()
→ fetch first value
→ isinstance check
→ sentinel comparison
→ generator termination
→ stdlib putheader()
```

## Change

Special-case the single-value path:

```python
if len(values) == 1:
    value = values[0]
    skip_header = isinstance(value, str) and value == SKIP_HEADER
else:
    skip_header = any(
        isinstance(value, str) and value == SKIP_HEADER for value in values
    )
```

The existing multi-value implementation is retained unchanged.

No request-generation logic outside the sentinel check is modified.

## Why this is safe

The change preserves the `isinstance(value, str)` guard added in #2141, so bytes values are never directly compared with the string `SKIP_HEADER` sentinel.

If the value is not `SKIP_HEADER`, the request still passes through the existing standard-library `putheader()` implementation. This means the existing validation of header names and values, including invalid newline handling, is unchanged.

The patch also introduces:

- no shared mutable state,
- no cache,
- no cross-request state,
- no new user-controlled execution path,
- no change to request framing.

## Behavioral boundary

The intended public behavior is unchanged.

The patch does not change:

- header ordering,
- header names or values,
- bytes-value handling,
- `SKIP_HEADER` semantics,
- invalid-header exceptions,
- `Content-Length` handling,
- `Transfer-Encoding` handling,
- chunked request framing,
- request bodies,
- connection behavior,
- the public API.

I also compared the baseline and optimized implementations directly for normal requests, skipped headers, bytes values, POST bodies, chunked requests, invalid header names and values, and unsupported `SKIP_HEADER` use.

The resulting request bytes or exception behavior were identical in all tested cases.

## Performance

The benchmark measures Python-side `HTTPConnection.request()` construction using an in-memory socket replacement, so network, DNS, TCP, and TLS latency are intentionally excluded.

Five independent runs were performed. Each measurement used repeated `timeit` samples for the baseline and optimized implementations.

| Workload | Median speedup | Approx. time saved |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4 headers | **1.097×** | **0.64 µs/request** |
| 12 headers | **1.128×** | **1.36 µs/request** |
| Mixed str/bytes headers | **1.092×** | **0.61 µs/request** |

All **15/15** baseline-versus-optimized comparisons were faster with the optimized implementation.

The larger improvement for the 12-header case is consistent with the mechanism: `putheader()` is called more times per request, so the removed generator/`any()` overhead accumulates.

These measurements apply specifically to Python-side request construction and are not intended as an end-to-end HTTP latency claim.

## Alternatives considered

### Keep the existing generator path for all calls

This keeps the implementation uniform, but retains avoidable generator and `any()` overhead for the dominant single-value case.

### Use `type(value) is str`

This was discussed historically when #2141 introduced the current bytes-safe check. The project retained `isinstance()` as the clearer Python-level check, and this patch does not need to change that decision.

### Restructure header/request generation more broadly

More aggressive changes could potentially remove additional Python overhead, but would touch request framing, ordering, or other security-sensitive behavior.

That would substantially increase correctness and review risk for a small additional optimization.

This patch therefore limits itself to the smallest common-case specialization that removes the measured overhead.

## Maintenance note

The optimization relies only on the existing `putheader(header, *values)` contract:

- a single supplied value can be checked directly;
- multiple values still require the existing general scan.

If the semantics of `values` or `SKIP_HEADER` change in the future, both branches should continue to apply the same sentinel-detection rule.

No HTTP protocol behavior is encoded into the fast path.

## Validation

Relevant request / connection / chunked tests:

```text
425 passed, 7 deselected
```

Formatting, linting, and typing:

```text
pyupgrade         passed
black             passed
isort             passed
flake8            passed
mypy              passed
git diff --check  passed
```

Broader local baseline-versus-patch testing produced the same failure set in both versions, with no failures introduced by this change.

Direct behavioral differential checks also confirmed identical request bytes or exceptions for:

```text
normal headers
bytes header values
SKIP_HEADER
POST bodies
chunked bodies
invalid header names
invalid header values
unsupported SKIP_HEADER usage
```

## Checklist

- [x] The redundant work is identified and isolated.
- [x] The optimization is limited to the common single-value path.
- [x] Multi-value behavior remains on the existing implementation.
- [x] Header validation is unchanged.
- [x] Request framing is unchanged.
- [x] Request wire output is unchanged in differential testing.
- [x] No new shared or mutable state is introduced.
- [x] Performance improvement is repeatable.
- [x] Performance claims are limited to the measured request-construction path.
- [x] Relevant tests, linting, formatting, and typing checks pass.

AI assistance was used during investigation, benchmarking, and review. I reviewed the final change and take responsibility for the implementation and claims above.
